html:
A wireframe is 5% interface and 95% conversation: it exists to get users to say "no, the button belongs here", and it is the cheapest place to discover that a whole workflow is backwards. This phase teaches you to sketch layouts that match user mental models, to translate the acceptance criteria you wrote in Phase 6 into interface elements, to validate behavior with clickable prototypes, and to turn approved mockups into requirements the delivery team can build. Everything below is applied to BrightLogistics' lead-rollout screens and to the repo's tab and layout metadata.

Learning Objectives

  • Sketch wireframes that reflect a user's mental model, not the developer's...
  • Map every acceptance criterion to a specific wireframe element before delivery...
  • Build clickable prototypes and run validation sessions that capture behavior, not opinions...
  • Keep prototypes cheap, grayscale, and disposable until the behavior is agreed...
  • Translate approved mockups into requirements, stories, and screenshot artifacts in the BRD...
  • Recognize when a Lightning page, dynamic form, or custom tab is the prototype...
  • Operate the repo's tabs/ and layout metadata as wireframe references...
  • Connect wireframe elements to the acceptance criteria they must survive delivery with...

1. Sketch for Conversation, Not for Production

A wireframe is a deliberately rough diagram of a page: boxes and labels, no colors, no real content, no font decisions. Its job is to move the conversation from "I like it" to "the routing button has to be visible before I open a lead", and that only works when the drawing is obviously disposable.

Keep wireframes rough on purpose. Sketch on paper or a whiteboard before any tool — the effort you put into a tool turns into the effort you defend against change. Grayscale and rough also keeps stakeholders commenting on structure and behavior, not taste and colors: when someone says "make the header blue", they have stopped testing the workflow and started decorating it.

Discipline of a good wireframe:

  • Boxes and labels only, no colors, no real content (use "Sample Value", not live accounts).
  • Number every element for discussion — W1, W2, W3 — so feedback is addressable: "move W4 to the top".
  • One wireframe per user goal, tied to one story, so the map of screens mirrors the story map.
  • Redraw fast; a rejected wireframe that took two minutes is cheap, one that took two hours is emotional.

2. Wireframe Anatomy: Elements and Annotations

Every screen is a stack of recognizable elements. Standardize them early so your drawings read at a glance:

ElementWhat it signalsExample in the lead record
Bounding boxA container regionThe record detail panel
Field label + valueData display or inputStatus, Source, Owner
Buttons / actionsA behavior the user can trigger"Route lead", "Log a call"
Filter controlA way to reduce the datasetSource dropdown above the queue list
Status badge / chipHigh-signal statePriority badge next to due date
Timeline / activity panelChronological historyActivity list sorted newest first

Annotate with a number and one line per element, and keep a matching legend on the page. The annotation is where the design intent becomes reviewable: "W2 — filter by Source; user may also filter by tier". That line, after agreement, is what becomes requirement text in section 11.

3. Tools and Techniques

Go from paper to a tool only when collaboration needs it. The spectrum:

  • Paper and whiteboard — instant, zero cost, the right start for almost everything; photograph the whiteboard before erasing.
  • Freeform dig whites — draw on the PDF of a real Salesforce page or on a screenshot — useful when the discussion is about placing elements on an existing layout.
  • Dedicated wireframe tools (e.g., Figma, Miro, Balsamiq) — when remote teams need the same artifact updated live; keep rendering plain and icons minimal.
  • Salesforce-native "wireframes" — the fastest trick: build a real Lightning record page with dynamic forms and freeform layout, rough, and show users the actual platform you will ship. This is a skill the repo supports directly (section 7).

Whatever the tool, the discipline stays: grayscale, numbered, disposable. The moment a wireframe tool does most of the thinking — colors, spacing, icons — the behavior discussion has lost. Polishing the wireframe is procrastination from the real feedback you need.

4. From Acceptance Criteria to Layout

Every acceptance criterion should visibly map to a wireframe element. A criterion with no home on the wireframe is either undefined behavior or a criterion nobody planned, and it will silently drift away during delivery — renegotiate it now, in the review, while change is cheap.

Acceptance criterionWireframe element
Lead with 3 activities shown newest-firstActivity timeline component
User can filter by sourceFilter dropdown above the list
High-priority cases highlightedPriority badge / color chip
Rep logs a call in < 5 secondsProminent "Log a call" action button

When you build a screen, walk each criterion one at a time and ask where the user will see it. If the criterion is "the dispatcher routes an inquiry to tier 1 within a minute" the wireframe must show the routing action in the record header, not buried in a menu — the element's position is the acceptance criterion. Name the pairing explicitly in the annotation line, e.g., "W4 — 'Route' action, satisfies AC 'route under 1 minute'".

The reverse check is just as valuable: every element you draw should answer to a criterion. An element with no criterion is scope you are about to build by accident. Where do you draw the element first? Start with the user's primary task — the highest-frequency goal (for BrightLogistics, route the lead and dispatch the load) — and place its actions as near to the top as sense allows.

5. Salesforce Tabs and Layouts: Where Wireframes Land

Inside Salesforce, what you wireframe becomes real metadata: tabs and page layouts. The repo ships the exact metadata you would touch:

  • Custom tabs for custom objects live in force-app/main/default/tabs/ — for example a tab that surfaces a Lightning app component.
  • Custom object tabs are declared on the object itself in force-app/main/default/objects/User_Story__c/ — the object's tab child entry that gives the backlog its own App Launcher home.
  • Page layouts are the object's layouts/ folder in the same metadata tree; these define which standard and custom fields appear on the record page in the traditional (non-Lightning) detail view.

A tab is a promise of a screen: one tab per user goal, named in the user's language, not the admin's. The BA's wireframe decisions map directly: "which objects deserve a tab", "which fields must appear on the record layout", "which related lists". Because tabs and layouts are in the repo you can deploy them to the lab and confirm the wireframe against the real org — wireframing with Salesforce-native artifacts (section 7) makes this the default.

6. Wireframes, Mockups, Prototypes: Know the Difference

Teams blur these three words and pay for it. Keep them strict:

ArtifactAnswersFidelityCost of change
WireframeWHERE things goGrayscale, roughVery low
MockupWHAT it looks likeVisual: color, type, spacingMedium
PrototypeHOW it FEELS to useClickable, scripted behaviorLow-to-medium, by design

A wireframe steers structure; a mockup steers appearance (and stands in for branding decisions and stakeholder sign-off on look); a prototype steers the behavior the user experiences — the sequence, the timing, the feedback. Do not polish the wireframe — polish the behavior. In most BA work you compress to two artifacts: rough wireframes for structure and a clickable prototype for behavior, with mockups reserved for the screens where look genuinely matters (market-facing pages).

7. Prototyping Inside Salesforce

The most convincing prototype is the real platform. Lightning pages are composable from standard and custom components, and dynamic forms render record fields from the page layout at runtime — so you can build a working-looking lead record page in minutes and show the user their actual future screen.

This is why the repo ships tabs and layouts as deployable metadata: deploy force-app/main/default/tabs/ and the User_Story__c tab metadata to the lab org, enable dynamic forms on the page, and your prototype is the sandbox UI sketch. Validation sessions run faster when the user clicks real components, real lookups, real save buttons — the hesitation and backtrack signals survive better than on a paper capture.

Keep the discipline even inside the platform: do not tune the layout first — put gross structure on the page, test it, then refine. Salesforce-native prototypes are the recommended default for Phase 15 mini projects because they double as deployable deliverables.

8. Clickable Prototypes and Validation Sessions

A clickable prototype strings 3-5 key screens together so a user can perform the actual journey. Then you run a validation session built on observation, not on testimonials:

  1. Link the happy path first — 3-5 screens is enough; the user should reach the goal.
  2. Let 3-5 real users click through WITHOUT instructions — resist narrating; the silence is the test.
  3. Watch where they hesitate, backtrack, or ask "how do I...?" — behavior is truth.
  4. Fix the prototype, re-test the fix with the same users, then lock screenshots of the agreed version into the BRD.
md
Validation session
- Task: "Route this inquiry to tier 1 within a minute"
- Observed: user could not FIND the routing action (buried in menu)
- Fix: move action to the record header
- Outcome: becomes requirement R-110 + story + wireframe W4

Capture three kinds of evidence: what the user does (clicks, hesitations, dead ends), what they say about it (the "I expected..."), and what changed between runs. Do not collect likes and dislikes as the goal — they tell you taste; observations tell you truth. One strong observed failure is worth a dozen compliments.

9. Conducting Validation Sessions with Stakeholders

Run the session like a mini experiment, especially with BrightLogistics' mixed audience of dispatchers (power users) and executives (decision makers):

  • Prepare one task story per screen, print or display in the tool.
  • Give each participant one clean copy and a quiet room; no leading hints beyond the first click.
  • Use thinking-aloud warmly: "say what you expect to happen next".
  • Time the key action (route under a minute, log a call under five seconds) — the acceptance criterion is your benchmark.
  • Group clusters of observations into themes, then into one proposed fix per theme.

Executives often want to skip the prototype and talk strategy. Invite them anyway but keep them on the task for the first ten minutes — their hesitation reveals exactly what a dispatcher could not find. The prototype is the equalizer.

10. From Approved Mockup to Requirement

An approved wireframe is a requirement waiting to be written. When the mockup locks, harvest it four ways:

  1. Screenshots with annotations become the appendix of the BRD — the agreed picture outlives the conversation in memory.
  2. Each numbered element with its pairing criterion becomes requirement lines — "W2, filter by Source: list in the queue page shows a Source filter above the grid".
  3. Each behavior discovered in validation (the routing action move) becomes requirement + story — exactly the R-110 pattern in section 8.
  4. The element-to-criterion map becomes a simple traceability table: Element, Acceptance criterion, Requirement ID, Story.

The key move: decisions made in the wireframe become named, traceable requirements, not vibes captured in screenshots. The repository pattern mirrors this — the User_Story__c record carries Acceptance_Criteria__c and the story's Status gate flow, so a wireframe agreement can update the story record the same day.

11. Common Pitfalls and BA Tips

  • Polishing the wireframe — colors and icons steal time from behavior feedback; stay rough until behavior is locked.
  • Unmapped criteria — an acceptance criterion with no element drifts away; run the reverse check and renegotiate.
  • Over-scripting validation — narrating the demo defeats the test; let the user act.
  • Mockup / prototype confusion — signing off the look and signing off the flow are different decisions; make them separate sessions.
  • Design by consensus — five opinions, one wireframe; the wireframe maps to criteria, not to whoever talks loudest.
  • Skipping the re-test — one fix unverified is two problems; re-test the fix with the same users.

Keep the golden rule: wireframes answer WHERE things go, prototypes answer HOW it FEELS, and until the behavior is validated, everything is disposable.

Hands-On Exercises

Exercise 8.1 — Wireframe the Lead Detail Screen from Acceptance Criteria

Steps:

  1. Take the three acceptance scenarios from Phase 6's exercise 6.2 (activity list).
  2. Sketch grayscale wireframes (paper or tool) for the lead record and the lead queue, numbering each element W1...Wn.
  3. Build the element-to-criteria table and mark any criterion without an element; renegotiate or re-slice it.

Expected result: two numbered wireframes plus a traceability table with no orphan criteria. What it proves: criteria drive layout and expose pre-existing scope gaps. (Match your answers to exercise 8.1 in Phase 15 which carries the same mapping task.)

Exercise 8.2 — Map a Tab into the Repo's Metadata

Steps:

  1. Open the custom-object tab entry under force-app/main/default/objects/User_Story__c/ and the tab definitions in force-app/main/default/tabs/.
  2. Decide the five tabs (one per primary user goal) BrightLogistics' app needs; for each, justify the named object it lands on.
  3. Deploy the tab metadata for the User_Story__c backlog tab to the lab org and find the App Launcher icon.

Expected result: a five-tab app plan and a deployed backlog tab. What it proves: a tab is a promise of a screen and layout metadata is the wireframe's real home.

Exercise 8.3 — Run a Validation Session and Re-Test the Fix

Steps:

  1. Link 3-5 wireframe screens into a clickable prototype (tool, or a Lightning page with dynamic forms in the lab).
  2. Run a validation session with 3-5 peers on the task "route this inquiry to tier 1 within a minute" — no hints, observe hesitations, think-aloud.
  3. Fix the single worst observed failure in the prototype, then re-run with the same users and compare time-to-route.

Expected result: a one-fix cycle with measurable before/after time, plus a harvested requirement + story. What it proves: observed behavior outranks expressed opinion, and one re-tested fix beats three rushed ones. (Prototype drills with scorecards appear in exercise 8.3 of Phase 15.)

Key Terms Glossary

TermDefinition
WireframeA rough grayscale layout answering WHERE things go.
MockupA visual design artifact answering WHAT it looks like.
PrototypeA clickable artifact answering HOW it feels to use.
Dynamic formA Lightning page component rendering record fields at runtime from the layout.
Page layoutThe object metadata defining which fields and related lists appear on the record detail.
Custom tabA user-facing entry point in the App Launcher for an object or app component.
Traceability tableThe map linking wireframe element, acceptance criterion, requirement, and story.
Validation sessionA structured observation of users acting on a prototype without instruction.
Think-aloudA user narrating expectations while interacting, revealing mental models.
Parking lotVisible capture of off-topic feedback for later triage.

Certification Checkpoints

  • Sketch a grayscale, numbered wireframe for a user goal and tie it to a story...
  • Map every acceptance criterion to a wireframe element and expose orphans...
  • Differentiate wireframe, mockup, and prototype and use each at the right time...
  • Run a validation session that records observed behavior, not stated opinion...
  • Translate an approved mockup into requirements, stories, and BRD screenshots...
  • Explain how Salesforce tabs, layouts, and dynamic forms act as real-platform prototypes...
  • Operate the repo's tabs/ and object tab metadata to drive the wireframe-to-deploy pipeline...

Summary

You can now run the whole visual pipeline: sketch rough wireframes for conversation, map acceptance criteria onto elements, prototype cheaply (including inside real Lightning pages), validate by observation, re-test one fix, and harvest the outcome into traceable requirements. The repo's tab and layout metadata lets you skip straight to the platform. This is the Requirements Elicitation skill that makes your Phase 10 reports measure a design people already agreed to — because you showed them the shape before building it.
